Anatomy-04.question: ১) Epicardium is another name of-
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is visceral pericardium. The epicardium is the outermost layer of the heart wall and is also called the visceral layer of serous pericardium.

Layers:

  1. Endocardium → Inner lining of heart chambers

  2. Myocardium → Cardiac muscle layer

  3. Epicardium → Visceral pericardium

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fibrous pericardium → Tough outer connective tissue layer surrounding the heart.

  • Serous pericardium → Has two layers:

    • Parietal layer

    • Visceral layer (epicardium)

  • Parietal pericardium → Lines the inner surface of fibrous pericardium.

High-yield point:

Heart wall:

  • Endocardium → inner

  • Myocardium → middle

  • Epicardium = visceral serous pericardium → outer

Exam pearl:
Epicardium = Visceral layer of serous pericardium.

Anatomy-04.question: ২) The pleura is a serous membrane which is lined by -
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is simple squamous epithelium. The pleura is a serous membrane lined by mesothelium, which is a type of simple squamous epithelium.

Functions of pleural mesothelium:

  • Provides a smooth, friction-free surface

  • Secretes pleural fluid

  • Allows easy movement of lungs during respiration

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Simple cuboidal epithelium → Found in structures like kidney tubules and small gland ducts.

  • Simple columnar epithelium → Found in gastrointestinal tract lining.

  • None of above → Incorrect because pleura is lined by simple squamous mesothelium.

High-yield point:

Serous membranes:

  • Pleura

  • Pericardium

  • Peritoneum

All are lined by mesothelium (simple squamous epithelium).

Exam pearl:
Pleura = mesothelium = simple squamous epithelium.

Anatomy-04.question: ৩) Base of the heart is formed by
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is the two atria. The base (posterior surface) of the heart is mainly formed by the left atrium, with a smaller contribution from the right atrium.

Key points:

  • Base of heart → Mainly left atrium + partly right atrium

  • It faces posteriorly toward the vertebral column.

  • The four pulmonary veins enter the left atrium at the base.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Left ventricle → Forms most of the left border and apex of the heart.

  • Right atrium → Contributes only a small part of the base.

  • The two ventricles → Mainly form the inferior surface and apex, not the base.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪) Right atrioventricular valve is known as the
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is Tricuspid valve. The right atrioventricular (AV) valve is the tricuspid valve, located between the right atrium and right ventricle.

Key points:

  • Tricuspid valve → Right atrium → Right ventricle

  • Has three cusps:

    • Anterior

    • Posterior

    • Septal

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Bicuspid valve → Another name for mitral valve; located between left atrium and left ventricle.

  • Mitral valve → Left atrioventricular valve.

  • Semilunar valve → Includes aortic and pulmonary valves; located at ventricular outflow tracts.

High-yield cardiac valves:

Valve Location
Tricuspid Right atrium → Right ventricle
Mitral (bicuspid) Left atrium → Left ventricle
Pulmonary Right ventricle → Pulmonary artery
Aortic Left ventricle → Aorta

Exam pearl:
Right AV valve = Tricuspid valve.

Anatomy-04.question: ৫) Largest vein of the heart-
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is coronary sinus. The coronary sinus is the largest venous channel of the heart and drains most of the venous blood from the myocardium into the right atrium.

Key points:

  • Located in the posterior atrioventricular groove

  • Receives:

    • Great cardiac vein

    • Middle cardiac vein

    • Small cardiac vein

    • Posterior cardiac veins

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Middle cardiac vein → Drains the inferior surface of the heart; smaller than coronary sinus.

  • Anterior cardiac veins → Drain directly into the right atrium; relatively small.

  • Great cardiac vein → Largest individual cardiac vein, but smaller than the coronary sinus.

High-yield cardiac venous drainage:

Myocardial veins → Coronary sinus → Right atrium

Exam pearl:
Largest vein of the heart = Coronary sinus.

Anatomy-04.question: ৬) Trachea is lined by -
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium. The trachea is lined by respiratory epithelium, which consists of:

  • Pseudostratified columnar epithelium

  • Ciliated cells

  • Goblet cells producing mucus

Functions:

  • Cilia move mucus and trapped particles upward (mucociliary clearance)

  • Goblet cells secrete mucus to trap dust and microbes

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ciliated stratified columnar epithelium → Not the typical lining of trachea.

  • Pseudostratified columnar epithelium (without cilia) → Incomplete; respiratory epithelium is characteristically ciliated.

  • Stratified columnar epithelium → Found in limited areas such as parts of large ducts, not trachea.

High-yield respiratory epithelium:

Site Epithelium
Trachea & bronchi Ciliated pseudostratified columnar + goblet cells
Alveoli Simple squamous epithelium
Oropharynx Stratified squamous epithelium

Exam pearl:
Trachea = ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium (respiratory epithelium).

Anatomy-04.question: ৭) Walls of vessel consist of-
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is All of above. The walls of a typical blood vessel consist of three layers (tunics):

  1. Tunica intima (inner layer)

    • Endothelium + connective tissue

    • Provides a smooth surface for blood flow

  2. Tunica media (middle layer)

    • Smooth muscle and elastic fibres

    • Controls vessel diameter and blood pressure

  3. Tunica adventitia (outer layer)

    • Connective tissue layer

    • Provides support and protection

The other options are incorrect because they represent only individual layers.

High-yield vessel wall:

Blood vessel wall =
Tunica intima + Tunica media + Tunica adventitia

Exam pearl:
Three layers of vessel wall → All of the above.

Anatomy-04.question: ৮) Vessel carry blood away from the heart to the organs and tissues is called-
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is Artery. An artery is a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart to organs and tissues.

Key features:

  • Carries blood away from the heart

  • Has thick, muscular, elastic walls

  • Blood flows under high pressure

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Vein → Carries blood towards the heart.

  • Capillary → Site of exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste products between blood and tissues.

  • Venule → Small vessel that collects blood from capillaries and joins to form veins.

High-yield recall:

A = Away from heart → Artery
V = Venous blood returns → Vein

Exam pearl:
Vessel carrying blood away from the heart = Artery.

Anatomy-04.question: ৯) Discontinuous capillaries (sinusoids) present in
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is Liver. Discontinuous capillaries (sinusoids) are specialized capillaries with:

  • Large gaps between endothelial cells

  • Discontinuous basement membrane

  • Allow passage of large molecules and cells

They are found in organs involved in filtration and exchange of large substances, such as:

  • Liver (hepatic sinusoids)

  • Spleen

  • Bone marrow

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Heart → Mainly has continuous capillaries.

  • Lung → Has continuous capillaries for efficient gas exchange.

  • Pancreas → Mainly has fenestrated capillaries (especially in endocrine islets).

High-yield capillary types:

Type Features Examples
Continuous Tight endothelial junctions Muscle, heart, lung, CNS
Fenestrated Small pores Kidney, endocrine glands, pancreas
Discontinuous (sinusoids) Large gaps, incomplete basement membrane Liver, spleen, bone marrow

Exam pearl:
Sinusoidal capillaries = Liver.

Anatomy-04.question: ১০) True end artery
Anatomy-04.option4: Arteries of kidneys lungs and the metaphysis of long bones
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is central artery of the retina. A true end artery is an artery that has no anastomosis with neighbouring arteries, so blockage causes complete ischaemia of its supplied area.

Examples of true end arteries:

  • Central artery of retina

  • Cerebral arteries (functionally end arteries)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Coronary arteries of the heart → Have anastomoses (though limited); considered functional end arteries.

  • Arteries of the spleen → Have collateral connections.

  • Arteries of kidneys, lungs and metaphysis of long bones → Generally considered functional end arteries, not true end arteries.

High-yield recall:

Type Example
True end artery Central artery of retina
Functional end artery Coronary arteries, renal arteries

Exam pearl:
Central artery of retina = true end artery.

Anatomy-04.question: ১১) Arteriole and precapillary sphincter are
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is resistance vessels. Arterioles and precapillary sphincters regulate blood flow into capillary beds by controlling vascular resistance.

Functions:

  • Control tissue perfusion

  • Regulate systemic blood pressure

  • Adjust blood flow according to metabolic needs

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Distribution vessels → Mainly arteries that distribute blood to different organs.

  • Exchange vessels → Capillaries where exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste occurs.

  • Capacitance or reservoir vessels → Veins, which store a large volume of blood.

High-yield classification of blood vessels:

Vessel type Main function
Arteries Distribution vessels
Arterioles + precapillary sphincters Resistance vessels
Capillaries Exchange vessels
Veins Capacitance/reservoir vessels

Exam pearl:
Arterioles = resistance vessels (main regulators of blood pressure).

Anatomy-04.question: ১২) Which regulates circadian rhythm?
১৩) Which hormone stimulates Osteoclast activity?
১৪) Secretion in what neuroendocrine cell is controlled directly by neural activity and involves a hormone that generally slows metabolic activity at night?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is pinealocyte. Pinealocytes are neuroendocrine cells of the pineal gland that secrete melatonin, a hormone whose secretion is directly controlled by neural activity from the circadian system.

Key points:

  • Light information → Retina → Suprachiasmatic nucleus → Sympathetic pathway → Pineal gland

  • Darkness stimulates pinealocytes to release melatonin

  • Melatonin helps regulate the sleep–wake cycle and generally reduces metabolic activity at night.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pituicyte → Glial cells of the posterior pituitary; support release of ADH and oxytocin.

  • Melanocyte → Produces melanin pigment in skin and other tissues.

  • Chromaffin cell → Neuroendocrine cell of adrenal medulla; secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline.

High-yield neuroendocrine cells:

Cell Hormone
Pinealocyte Melatonin
Chromaffin cell Adrenaline/Noradrenaline
Pituicyte Supports ADH/Oxytocin release

Exam pearl:
Neural control + night hormone regulating circadian rhythm = Pinealocyte → Melatonin.

Anatomy-04.question: ১৫) Capillaries only have
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is endothelium. Capillaries are the simplest blood vessels and consist only of a single layer of endothelial cells resting on a basement membrane.

Structure of capillary:

  • Endothelium

  • Basement membrane

They do not have:

  • Tunica media

  • Tunica adventitia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Intima → Present as a distinct layer in larger vessels; capillary endothelium is considered a specialized part of intima.

  • Media → Absent in capillaries.

  • Adventitia → Absent in capillaries.

High-yield vessel wall:

Vessel Layers
Artery/Vein Intima + Media + Adventitia
Capillary Endothelium + basement membrane only

Exam pearl:
Capillaries contain only endothelium.

Anatomy-04.question: ১৬) Which of the following components increase(s) as a proportion of the respiratory tract wall from trachea to alveoli?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is elastic fibres. As the respiratory tract branches from the trachea to alveoli, the proportion of elastic tissue increases, which helps maintain airway patency and allows alveolar recoil during expiration.

Changes from trachea → alveoli:

  • Elastic fibres ↑

    • Important for lung elasticity and recoil

  • Cilia ↓ and disappear

    • Present in trachea/bronchi, absent in alveoli

  • Cartilage ↓ and disappears

    • Present in trachea and bronchi, absent in bronchioles and alveoli

  • Smooth muscle changes

    • Becomes relatively more prominent in bronchioles but not the best answer for overall tract wall proportion.

High-yield respiratory histology:

Structure Trachea Alveoli
Cartilage Present Absent
Cilia Numerous Absent
Elastic fibres Less More
Smooth muscle Present Minimal

Exam pearl:
From trachea → alveoli: elastic fibres increase, cartilage and cilia decrease.

Anatomy-04.question: ১৭) Which structural feature distinguishes between terminal and respiratory bronchioles?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is alveoli. The main structural difference between terminal bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles is the presence of alveoli.

  • Terminal bronchioles

    • Last part of the conducting zone

    • No alveoli in their walls

    • Lined by ciliated cuboidal epithelium with club cells

  • Respiratory bronchioles

    • First part of the respiratory zone

    • Alveoli open from their walls

    • Participate in gas exchange

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cilia → Present in both terminal and respiratory bronchioles (although reduced distally).

  • Exocrine bronchiolar cells (club cells) → Present in both.

  • Mucous glands in lamina propria → Absent in bronchioles; found in larger airways.

High-yield respiratory airway sequence:

Terminal bronchiole → Respiratory bronchiole → Alveolar duct → Alveolar sac

Exam pearl:
Respiratory bronchiole = bronchiole with alveoli in its wall.

Anatomy-04.question: ১৮) Which hormone suppresses immune cell activities?
১৯) Secretion, chemical modification and storage, reuptake, and digestion of a protein occur in epithelial cells of what endocrine tissue?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is thyroid gland. Thyroid follicular epithelial cells are involved in:

  • Secretion of thyroglobulin protein

  • Chemical modification (iodination of tyrosine residues in thyroglobulin)

  • Storage (thyroglobulin stored in colloid)

  • Reuptake of thyroglobulin by follicular cells

  • Digestion (proteolysis) to release thyroid hormones (T3 and T4)

This unique process occurs in thyroid follicles.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) → Stores and releases ADH and oxytocin produced in hypothalamus; not involved in protein modification/storage.

  • Adrenal medulla → Chromaffin cells secrete catecholamines (adrenaline and noradrenaline).

  • Adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary) → Produces peptide hormones but does not store and process a protein in this follicular manner.

High-yield thyroid physiology:

Thyroid follicular cell → Thyroglobulin synthesis → Iodination → Colloid storage → Endocytosis → Proteolysis → T3/T4 release

Exam pearl:
Protein synthesis + iodination + colloid storage + reuptake = Thyroid gland.

Anatomy-04.question: ২০) Rare cell type in pancreatic islets
২১) A glucagonoma is a malignant tumor consisting of what cells?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is A (alpha) cells. A glucagonoma is a tumour of the pancreatic α cells of the islets of Langerhans, which secrete excessive glucagon.

Clinical features of glucagonoma:

  • Hyperglycaemia/diabetes mellitus

  • Weight loss

  • Necrolytic migratory erythema (classic skin lesion)

  • Anaemia

  • Glossitis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • B or β cells → Tumour causes excess insulin secretion (insulinoma).

  • Chromophils → Cells of the anterior pituitary/adrenal medulla, not pancreatic islet cells.

  • D or δ cells → Secrete somatostatin; tumour = somatostatinoma.

High-yield pancreatic endocrine tumours:

Tumour Cell type Hormone
Glucagonoma α cells Glucagon
Insulinoma β cells Insulin
Somatostatinoma δ cells Somatostatin
VIPoma Enterochromaffin/neuroendocrine cells VIP

Exam pearl:
Glucagonoma = α-cell tumour → ↑ glucagon.

Anatomy-04.question: ২২) Layer of adrenal cortex close to medulla
২৩) Oxiphil cells are present in
২৪) What tissue is directly associated with and extends into the heart valves?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is cardiac skeleton. The cardiac skeleton is a framework of dense connective tissue that is directly associated with the heart valves and extends into the valve cusps.

Functions of cardiac skeleton:

  • Supports the cardiac valves

  • Provides attachment for cardiac muscle fibres

  • Electrically insulates atria from ventricles (except through AV bundle of His)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Myocardium → Cardiac muscle layer; forms the main wall of the heart but does not extend into valves.

  • Epicardium → Outer layer of the heart wall; not associated with valve structure.

  • Atrioventricular bundle of His → Conducting tissue that passes through the cardiac skeleton, but it is not the tissue forming the valves.

High-yield cardiac anatomy:

Cardiac skeleton = fibrous rings + fibrous trigones

  • Supports tricuspid, mitral, aortic, and pulmonary valves

  • Provides electrical insulation between atria and ventricles

Exam pearl:
Heart valves are extensions of the cardiac skeleton (fibrous connective tissue).

Anatomy-04.question: ২৫) Which bone accommodates pituitary gland?
২৬) Which feature involved in protection of the respiratory tract is absent from the digestive tract?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is cilia. Cilia are a specialized protective feature of the respiratory tract that help remove inhaled particles and microorganisms by mucociliary clearance.

Function:

  • Cilia move mucus containing trapped dust and pathogens toward the pharynx for removal.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Goblet cells → Present in both respiratory and digestive tracts; secrete mucus.

  • Lymphoid nodules → Present in both:

    • Respiratory tract (e.g., BALT)

    • Digestive tract (e.g., Peyer's patches)

  • Secretory IgA → Present in mucosal surfaces of both respiratory and digestive tracts as immune protection.

High-yield mucosal defence:

Feature Respiratory tract Digestive tract
Goblet cells Present Present
Cilia Present Absent
Lymphoid tissue Present Present
Secretory IgA Present Present

Exam pearl:
Cilia are the key protective feature unique to the respiratory tract.

Anatomy-04.question: ২৭) The pulmonary (functional) and bronchial (nutritive) arterial systems enter the lungs separately at the hilus but anastomose into a single system at which level?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is respiratory bronchioles. The pulmonary (functional) circulation and bronchial (nutritional) circulation enter the lung separately at the hilum, but they anastomose at the level of respiratory bronchioles.

Key points:

  • Pulmonary arteries → carry deoxygenated blood for gas exchange in alveoli.

  • Bronchial arteries → supply oxygenated blood to bronchial walls and supporting tissues.

  • Their connections occur mainly in the distal airway region, especially respiratory bronchioles.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Larynx → Supplied by branches of external and internal carotid arteries; not the site of pulmonary–bronchial anastomosis.

  • Terminal bronchioles → Part of conducting zone; anastomosis occurs more distally.

  • Segmental bronchioles → Not the main site of this vascular connection.

High-yield respiratory circulation:

Pulmonary circulation → alveoli (gas exchange)
Bronchial circulation → airway walls (nutrition)
Anastomosis → respiratory bronchioles

Exam pearl:
Pulmonary and bronchial arterial systems unite at respiratory bronchioles.

Anatomy-04.question: ২৮) Part of posterior pituitary
২৯) Impression exclusive for medial surface of right lung
৩০) Right lung
৩১) Which capillaries allow cells and plasma proteins to enter or leave their lumen?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is sinusoidal capillaries (discontinuous capillaries). These capillaries have:

  • Large gaps between endothelial cells

  • Incomplete or absent basement membrane

  • Wide lumen

They allow the passage of:

  • Blood cells

  • Large plasma proteins

  • Large molecules

Examples:

  • Liver

  • Spleen

  • Bone marrow

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Continuous capillaries → Have tight endothelial junctions; allow small molecules but restrict cells and large proteins.

  • Fenestrated capillaries → Have pores (fenestrae); allow increased exchange of small molecules but generally not cells.

  • Anastomotic capillaries → Refers to vascular connections, not a capillary type for cell passage.

High-yield capillary types:

Type Feature Example
Continuous Tight junctions Muscle, lung, CNS
Fenestrated Small pores Kidney, endocrine glands
Sinusoidal Large gaps → cells & proteins pass Liver, spleen, bone marrow

Exam pearl:
Capillaries allowing cells and plasma proteins to pass = Sinusoidal capillaries.

Anatomy-04.question: ৩২) Chromaffin cells are present in
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is adrenal medulla. Chromaffin cells are specialized neuroendocrine cells located in the adrenal medulla that secrete catecholamines:

  • Adrenaline (epinephrine)

  • Noradrenaline (norepinephrine)

Key points:

  • Derived from neural crest cells

  • Act as modified sympathetic postganglionic neurons

  • Stimulated by sympathetic preganglionic fibres

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Adrenal cortex → Contains zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis; secretes steroid hormones.

  • Parathyroid gland → Contains chief cells and oxyphil cells; secretes PTH.

  • Neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) → Contains pituicytes and stores/releases ADH and oxytocin.

High-yield endocrine histology:

Location Cell Hormone
Adrenal medulla Chromaffin cells Adrenaline & noradrenaline
Adrenal cortex Cortical cells Steroid hormones
Parathyroid Chief cells

Anatomy-04.question: ৩৩) Butterfly shaped gland
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is thyroid gland. The thyroid gland is butterfly-shaped and is located in the anterior neck, below the larynx.

Key features:

  • Consists of:

    • Two lateral lobes

    • Central isthmus connecting the lobes

  • Produces:

    • Thyroxine (T4)

    • Triiodothyronine (T3)

    • Calcitonin (from parafollicular C cells)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Adrenal gland → Triangular/crescent-shaped glands located above kidneys.

  • Parathyroid gland → Small, oval glands on the posterior surface of thyroid.

  • Pituitary gland → Pea-sized, oval gland located in the sella turcica.

High-yield anatomy:

Butterfly-shaped gland = Thyroid gland

Exam pearl:
Neck butterfly gland → Thyroid.

Anatomy-04.question: ৩৪) What feature does cardiac muscle possess that is missing in skeletal muscle?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is intercalated discs. Cardiac muscle cells have intercalated discs, which are specialized junctions connecting adjacent cardiac myocytes.

Functions of intercalated discs:

  • Provide mechanical attachment between cells (desmosomes, fascia adherens)

  • Allow electrical communication (gap junctions)

  • Enable coordinated contraction of the heart

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Striations → Present in both cardiac and skeletal muscle.

  • Multiple nuclei → Skeletal muscle fibres are typically multinucleated; cardiac muscle usually has one central nucleus (sometimes two).

  • Voluntary control → Skeletal muscle is voluntary; cardiac muscle is involuntary.

High-yield muscle differences:

Feature Cardiac muscle Skeletal muscle
Striations Present Present
Nuclei 1–2 central Multiple peripheral
Control Involuntary Voluntary
Intercalated discs Present Absent

Exam pearl:
Unique feature of cardiac muscle = Intercalated discs.

Anatomy-04.question: ৩৫) Important in bronchoconstriction & bronchodialatation?
৩৬) Which one is site of phonation?
৩৭) Respiratory zone excludes
৩৮) Location of fenestrated capillaries
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is anterior pituitary. Fenestrated capillaries have small pores (fenestrae) in their endothelial lining, allowing rapid exchange of hormones and other substances.

Common sites of fenestrated capillaries:

  • Anterior pituitary

  • Endocrine glands

  • Kidney glomeruli

  • Intestinal villi

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Liver → Contains sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries.

  • Spleen → Contains sinusoidal capillaries.

  • Choroid plexus → Contains specialized fenestrated capillaries, but the blood–CSF barrier is maintained by ependymal cells. In standard histology MCQs, the anterior pituitary is a classic example of fenestrated capillaries.

Anatomy-04.question: ৩৯) Which of the following accurately describes glucocorticoids?
Anatomy-04.option2: Are produced in response to stimulation by ACTH
Anatomy-04.option3: Are produced primarily by the zone glomerulosa
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is glucocorticoids are produced in response to ACTH stimulation.

Key points:

  • Glucocorticoids (mainly cortisol) are produced by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex.

  • Their secretion is regulated by the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis:

    • CRH (hypothalamus) → ACTH (pituitary) → cortisol (adrenal cortex)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Include the steroid hormone aldosterone 

    • Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid, produced by zona glomerulosa.

  • Are produced primarily by the zona glomerulosa 

    • Zona glomerulosa produces mineralocorticoids (aldosterone).

  • Typically enhance the immune response

    • Glucocorticoids are immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory.

High-yield adrenal cortex:

Zone Hormone Regulation
Zona glomerulosa Aldosterone RAAS + K⁺
Zona fasciculata Cortisol (glucocorticoid) ACTH
Zona reticularis Androgens ACTH

Mnemonic:
GFR = Salt, Sugar, Sex

  • Glomerulosa → Salt (aldosterone)

  • Fasciculata → Sugar (cortisol)

  • Reticularis → Sex hormones

Exam pearl:
ACTH stimulates glucocorticoid (cortisol) secretion from zona fasciculata.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪০) What hormone is produced in response to decreased blood calcium levels?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is Parathyroid hormone (PTH). Decreased blood calcium levels stimulate the parathyroid glands to release PTH.

Actions of PTH:

  • ↑ Bone resorption → releases calcium into blood

  • ↑ Calcium reabsorption in kidneys

  • ↑ Activation of vitamin D → ↑ intestinal calcium absorption

The overall effect is increase in serum calcium level.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pancreatic polypeptide → Regulates pancreatic and gastrointestinal functions.

  • Somatostatin → Inhibits secretion of growth hormone, insulin, glucagon, and GI hormones.

  • Calcitonin → Released when blood calcium is high; lowers calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity.

Exam pearl:
Low serum calcium → Parathyroid hormone secretion.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪১) Features of arteries
৪২) Pulmonary trunk is developed from
৪৩) Which endocrine gland acts without pituitary control?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is parathyroid gland. The parathyroid gland functions independently of pituitary control.

Regulation:

  • Parathyroid chief cells directly sense blood calcium levels.

  • ↓ Serum calcium → ↑ PTH secretion

  • ↑ Serum calcium → ↓ PTH secretion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thyroid → Controlled by TSH from the anterior pituitary (via TRH from hypothalamus).

  • Adrenal cortex → Glucocorticoid and androgen secretion are regulated by ACTH.

  • Ovary → Controlled by FSH and LH from the anterior pituitary.

High-yield endocrine control:

Gland Pituitary control
Thyroid TSH
Adrenal cortex ACTH
Ovary FSH/LH
Parathyroid No pituitary control; regulated by Ca²⁺ level

Exam pearl:
Endocrine gland independent of pituitary = Parathyroid gland.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৪) Which description is true of continuous capillaries?
Anatomy-04.option2: Most common in both brain and muscle
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is most common in both brain and muscle. Continuous capillaries are the most common type of capillary and are found in:

  • Skeletal muscle

  • Cardiac muscle

  • Brain (blood–brain barrier type)

Features of continuous capillaries:

  • Continuous endothelial lining

  • Complete basement membrane

  • Small intercellular clefts

  • Allow passage of small molecules (water, ions, glucose, oxygen)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Unusually wide lumens 
    → Characteristic of sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries.

  • Abundant fenestrations
    → Characteristic of fenestrated capillaries (e.g., kidney, endocrine glands).

  • Lack a complete basement membrane 
    → Seen in sinusoidal capillaries.

High-yield capillary types:

Type Features Examples
Continuous Complete basement membrane Brain, muscle, lung
Fenestrated Pores/fenestrae Kidney, endocrine glands
Sinusoidal Large gaps, incomplete basement membrane Liver, spleen, bone marrow

Exam pearl:
Continuous capillaries = most common; found in brain and muscle.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৫) During light microscopic examination of a tissue, you note a vessel that has no smooth muscle but a large amount of connective tissue at its periphery. Which of the following vessels are you examining?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is venule. Venules have little or no smooth muscle and a relatively large amount of connective tissue (adventitia) compared with their thin wall.

Key features of venules:

  • Formed by the union of capillaries

  • Thin endothelial lining

  • Little or no tunica media (smooth muscle)

  • Prominent connective tissue in larger venules

  • Site of leukocyte migration during inflammation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Arteriole ❌

    • Has a prominent smooth muscle layer (tunica media) that regulates blood flow.

  • Elastic artery ❌

    • Has abundant elastic fibres and thick smooth muscle layers.

  • Capillary ❌

    • Consists only of endothelium + basement membrane; lacks a connective tissue periphery.

High-yield vessel histology:

Vessel Main feature
Arteriole Smooth muscle dominant
Venule No/very little smooth muscle + connective tissue
Capillary Endothelium only
Elastic artery Elastic lamellae

Exam pearl:
Thin wall + no smooth muscle + connective tissue around vessel = Venule.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৬) Which marks the junction between the trabeculated part and smooth part of the right atrium?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is crista terminalis. The crista terminalis is a muscular ridge in the right atrium that marks the junction between:

  • Trabeculated part (rough part) → derived from primitive atrium; contains pectinate muscles

  • Smooth part (sinus venarum) → derived from sinus venosus; receives venae cavae and coronary sinus

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Trabeculae carneae 

    • Found in the ventricles, not the atrium.

  • Fossa ovalis 

    • Depression in the interatrial septum; remnant of foramen ovale.

  • Conus arteriosus 

    • Smooth outflow tract of the right ventricle.

High-yield right atrium anatomy:

Structure Function
Crista terminalis Separates smooth and rough parts of right atrium
Pectinate muscles Rough part of atrium
Sinus venarum Smooth part of right atrium
Fossa ovalis Remnant of fetal foramen ovale

Exam pearl:
Right atrium smooth–rough junction = Crista terminalis

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৭) Which cardiac vein drains directly into Right atrium?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is anterior cardiac veins. Unlike most cardiac veins, the anterior cardiac veins drain directly into the right atrium.

Key points:

  • Arise from the anterior wall of the right ventricle

  • Open directly into the right atrium

  • Do not drain through the coronary sinus

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Great cardiac vein 

    • Drains into the coronary sinus.

  • Middle cardiac vein 

    • Drains into the coronary sinus.

  • Small cardiac vein 

    • Drains into the coronary sinus.

High-yield cardiac venous drainage:

Most cardiac veins → Coronary sinus → Right atrium

Exception:
Anterior cardiac veins → Directly into right atrium

Exam pearl:
Cardiac vein draining directly into right atrium = Anterior cardiac vein.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৮) The RCA branches into the following except
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is Anterior interventricular (IV) artery. The right coronary artery (RCA) does not give rise to the anterior IV artery.

The anterior interventricular artery (LAD) is a branch of the left coronary artery.

Branches of the RCA include:

  • SA nodal artery (usually)

  • Right marginal artery

  • AV nodal artery

  • Posterior interventricular (IV) artery (in right-dominant circulation)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • SA nodal artery  → Common branch of RCA.

  • AV nodal artery → Usually arises from RCA.

  • Posterior IV artery → Usually arises from RCA.

High-yield coronary artery branches:

Coronary artery Major branches
RCA SA nodal, AV nodal, right marginal, posterior IV artery
LCA LAD (anterior IV), circumflex

Exam pearl:
Anterior interventricular artery (LAD) = branch of left coronary artery, not RCA.

Anatomy-04.question: ৪৯) The vertebral level where trachea ends
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is T4. The trachea bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi at the level of the sternal angle, which corresponds to:

  • T4–T5 vertebral level (commonly asked as T4)

This point is called the carina.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • C5  → Level of pharynx–larynx region, not tracheal termination.

  • C6  → Beginning of trachea (lower border of cricoid cartilage).

  • T5→ May be included in the T4–T5 range, but the classic exam answer is T4.

High-yield trachea levels:

Event Vertebral level
Beginning of trachea C6
Tracheal bifurcation (carina) T4–T5 (sternal angle)

Exam pearl:
Trachea ends at the carina → T4 level.

Anatomy-04.question: ৫০) Vasa vasorum serve a function analogous to that of which of the following?
Anatomy-04.exp:
The correct answer is coronary arteries. Vasa vasorum are small blood vessels that supply the walls of large blood vessels (especially large arteries and veins) because diffusion from the lumen is insufficient.

Their function is analogous to the coronary arteries, which supply the myocardium of the heart.

Key points:

  • Found mainly in:

    • Large arteries (e.g., aorta)

    • Large veins

  • Supply:

    • Outer tunica media

    • Tunica adventitia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Valves → Prevent backflow of blood in veins.

  • Basal lamina  → Supports endothelial cells and forms part of the basement membrane.

  • Endothelial diaphragms  → Found in fenestrated capillaries and regulate exchange.

High-yield vessel wall:

Vasa vasorum = "vessels of vessels"
→ Supply the walls of large vessels, similar to how coronary arteries supply heart muscle.

Exam pearl:
Vasa vasorum function is analogous to coronary arteries.
